questions.q: Why does this lesson use the financial-debt metaphor to describe shipping a quick solution under deadline pressure?
options: Because technical debt always carries the same fixed penalty regardless of context, just like a late fee
Because, like financial debt, it can be a good decision (a known cost with a plan to repay it) or a bad one (an untracked liability that compounds), depending on whether it was taken on deliberately
Because Salesforce literally charges interest on deferred configuration work
Because the metaphor only applies to custom Apex code, never to declarative shortcuts
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames debt as a neutral financial tool -- good or bad depending on whether the team knows what was deferred, has a plan to pay it down, and whether the ongoing cost is smaller than the value of shipping on time.

questions.q: What is the actual difference between deliberate and accidental technical debt, per this lesson?
options: Deliberate debt is always cheaper to fix than accidental debt
Accidental debt only occurs in declarative tools like Flow, never in Apex
Deliberate debt is explicitly named and documented at the time it's taken on, while accidental debt is built as if it were the permanent design, with no record of what was deferred or why
There is no real difference -- both terms describe the same thing
questions.explain: The cost in the code itself can be identical either way -- what differs is whether a future team knows the limitation was intentional and tracked, or has no way to tell whether it was an oversight.

questions.q: In the hardcoded Record Type example, what makes the shortcut a mistake rather than a reasonable tradeoff, per this lesson?
options: Hardcoding Record Types is always wrong regardless of context
The company has fewer than three business units
The team used a validation rule instead of a Flow
The team takes the shortcut despite already knowing the company is acquiring two more business units next year, meaning the 'debt' was never going to be small or short-lived
questions.explain: The same shortcut can be the right call for a team with no credible plan to add a fourth business unit, and a mistake dressed up as a shortcut for a team that already knows expansion is coming -- context is what determines which.

questions.q: Which of these does this lesson list as a real criterion for deciding how much long-term investment a given shortcut deserves?
options: Whether the deadline is real and what's actually lost if it slips, and how likely and how soon the scenario the shortcut doesn't handle actually is
Whether the development team personally prefers writing Apex or Flow
Whether the shortcut can be implemented using only standard objects
Whether the org has more than 1,000 Salesforce licenses
questions.explain: The lesson lists the realness of the deadline and the likelihood/timing of the scenario the shortcut fails to handle as two of the concrete criteria for sizing how risky a given piece of debt actually is.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should a mature architect do about technical debt, rather than avoiding it entirely?
options: Gold-plate every feature regardless of whether speed actually matters, to avoid ever taking on debt
Take debt deliberately when justified, name it explicitly (for example in an ADR), and track it the same way any other tradeoff is tracked
Refuse to ship anything until every feature is built to its most scalable, configurable version
Let each developer decide individually whether to document a shortcut, with no consistent practice
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls avoiding all debt its own mistake (gold-plating) and instead recommends taking debt deliberately and documenting it, connecting directly back to the ADR practice from Lesson 8.
